effect: An AI government now judges recession on three months of output, not one. Each month the AI's budget policy compared real output with the month before, and a fall of a tenth of a percent put it in 'support' (recession) mode: it may not raise taxes or cut spending that month, even with a large deficit, and a mid-review switch into support overrides the current plan, so one month's noise could block budget repair, and one up month inside a real downturn switched support off. Now the test compares the average real output of the last three months with the three months before (from the game's own twelve-month output history), with the same 0.1% margin; when that history is missing, or any of those six months is not a positive number, the old one-month test is used. Measured on an unmodded 12-month run of this game version (real output, all AI countries, months 6 to 12): in months when output was higher than a year earlier both tests fire about equally often (9.1% one-month, 8.5% three-month), but in months when output was lower than a year earlier the three-month test calls recession in 77% of them against 50% for the one-month test, so the change mostly stops real downturns being missed. Real-world behaviour: fiscal stimulus answers a downturn that shows over a quarter or more (the usual recession test is output falling over successive quarters), not one month's noise. Crisis mode, the two-month 'consolidation not working' rule and the rest of the budget rules are unchanged. Day-0 effect: none on day 0 itself (the review does not run then). The first review can run within the first days, when the twelve-month history still holds the game's start-up trend built from each country's growth rate, so a country seeded with output falling by about 0.4% a year or more starts in support mode, as the old fallback (growth below -0.5%) roughly did; the history fills with simulated months over the first half year. No new saved state: the ratio is recomputed from saved output history at every review.
